paragraphs: R' Yannai (a Tanna), father of R' Dostai.

This R' Yannai is the Tanna mentioned in Avot ch. 4, mishnah 15, who said: "We have no [understanding] of either the tranquility of the wicked or the sufferings of the righteous." Hyman considers it very likely that what was said in the Yerushalmi, Taanit ch. 4, halakhah 2 — Rabbi Levi said: "They found a scroll of genealogies in Jerusalem, and it was written in it: Rabbi Yanai from the family of Eli" — refers to this Tannaitic R' Yannai, since R' Yannai the Amora lived a long life, as explained in his entry. Moreover, he argues, the entire scroll mentions Tannaim and not Amoraim, and in the days of R' Yannai the Amora it would not be appropriate to say "they found it in Jerusalem." And in the Tosefta, Sanhedrin ch. 2: R' Yannai in the name of Rashbag.

He was the father of R' Dostai who is mentioned in Eruvin ch. 5, mishnah 4, in the name of R' Dostai son of R' Yannai (a student of R' Meir and a colleague of Rabbi, as explained in his entry). Likewise, Hyman says, it appears that R' Elazar son of R' Yannai is a son of this R' Yannai. Hyman says that הכ״ופ in chapter 1 meant this R' Yannai and R' Dostai (his son), in reporting his received tradition that they were buried in the town of Akhbara.

notes.text: The genealogical scroll in the named Taanit4:2 paragraph reads “of Eli,” not Ula. That paragraph also names Rabbi Chiyya the Great; Hyman’s statement that the scroll contains only tannaim is his argument, not a claim this review has verified. The work abbreviated הכ״ופ remains to be checked rather than invented.

The Taanit paragraph explicitly has Rabbi Levi and Rabbi Yanai from those of Eli, and separately Rabbi Chiyya the Great; those two full personal titles are supported only inside the quoted paragraph. The supplied heading and other abbreviated Yannai, Dostai, Elazar and Meir occurrences retain R'; full Rabbi in colleague of Rabbi remains explicit and is not converted into a newly bound person. Avot4:15 and Eruvin5:4 are Hyman's supplied locators; the older Avot Torat Emet quotation is historical evidence, not a newly reread whole Avot scalar here. Rashbag remains abbreviated in the body; its conventional Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel expansion in the older note is not fresh title or identity evidence for the uninspected Tosefta passage. The Taanit form is Yanai/יניי in the supplied quotation beside Yannai/ינאי elsewhere; neither the names nor the supplied Hebrew are harmonized. Of Eli is supported by the named digital wording, not by a printed-pixel collation or correction history, and the old Ula guess remains archived. Hyman's very likely identification, long life of the Amora, argument that all persons in the scroll are Tannaim and not Amoraim, and argument about finding it in Jerusalem retain their stated force as Hyman's reasoning, not an accepted chronology or identity. The statement that Elazar appears to be this Yannai's son stays tentative and attributed, while Hyman's unqualified father-of-Dostai report remains unqualified as a source statement. The printed notice (volume II, p. 765) retains הכ״ופ and chapter 1. A separately consulted public digital Kaftor VaFerach, chapter 11, reports a received tradition naming Yannai, Dostai and Nehorai south of Akhbara. Its page is explicitly marked incomplete and unproofread. This is a direct named comparison for the burial tradition, not a collation of Hyman’s chapter 1 printing or proof of which Yannai he intended. The earlier failed Sefaria request was not repeated; the newly read public digital witness supplements the old inspection limit. Seder HaDorot’s different citation and its express uncertainty about which Yannai remain distinct. Jerusalem Talmud Taanit 4:2 names Yannai of Eli and also Chiyya the Great; Hyman’s very likely identification and his argument that the scroll contains only Tannaim remain his reasoning. Avot 4:15 confirms the saying with both negatives; Eruvin 5:4 names Dostai bar Rabbi Yannai quoting Rabbi Meir, without independently binding that father to this notice or establishing the colleague identification. The consulted Tosefta Sanhedrin 2 names Yannai quoting Rashbag. Hyman’s unqualified father-of-Dostai assertion and his tentative suggestion about Elazar retain their differing force. The supplied Hebrew, abbreviated titles, work siglum, existing notes and cross-entry uncertainty remain unchanged.
